title: I built a roguelite space shooter with Claude Code, and the trailer is the game filming itself
author: azzaisme
selftext:
*Not everyone comes home.*

The Cost of Stars is an arena roguelite I’ve been building in Godot with Claude Code doing almost all of the programming. You run a forward station holding off a swarm. Every run is a different pilot, and when one dies their name goes on the Wall and Earth sends you the next one. The station’s crew send supply pods with upgrade cards between fights, and there are four bosses, including Steve, who is not as dead as he looks.

The part I most wanted to share is the trailer. There’s no screen recording and no editing in it. Claude wrote a “director” script that plays the actual game: it launches the ship, flies the fights, opens pods, kills a pilot and triggers the boss entrances, with its own cinematic camera on top. Godot’s Movie Maker records it at a locked 60 fps, so every render is identical. That changed how I give feedback. Instead of re-editing, I’d watch a render and say things like “the pilot should be visible before they get in the ship” or “I just watched the pilot throw a bomb at nothing”, and it became a code change and a re-render. Steve’s wink at the end took three passes before he opened both eyes, winked, and went back to playing dead.

On the workflow: the game has gone through roughly 850 GitHub issues and PRs, one branch each, and nothing merges until it passes a big automated smoke suite. That's a headless run of the real game checking everything from boss attacks to save files. Honestly, that suite is the only reason I trust the AI’s code at this scale. I often have several Claude sessions working on different issues at once, and they literally message each other to take turns running Godot, because two runs at once break the timing checks.

What surprised me: plain-language playtest notes work really well. “That reads as the Gate”, “the lighting on the logo sucks”, and my favourite, “Ew, that’s far too Hades”, which turned a fountain into a garage on a moon. It’s strongest at systems and tests. Where it slips is shipping something that’s technically correct but looks wrong. The trailer’s first cut had the camera lovingly filming an empty room, and the first mp4 wouldn’t open on Windows. I still have to watch everything.

The art is Claude Design with my "style", the music is CC0 from OpenGameArt (MintoDog, yd) and StockTune, and the sound effects are Kenney’s packs plus synthesis. The voices are AI placeholders until I can pay real actors, so the trailer only uses my "WAH WAH"

It’s built for Steam Deck/windows/mobile and I've tested it on all. Coming soon.
